body_markdown:
When I saw the film *Chitty Chitty Bang Bang* for the first time, at the age of seven, my fate as a car guy was sealed. Cars were already at the center of my life: Dad worked at Chevrolet in Flint, and his dad ran the Texaco gas station in my rural hometown. I was already predisposed toward being car crazy in the same way some people inherit the color of their eyes or hair. Then came Chitty.


The old-fashioned race cars roared across the screen of our family’s television on Thanksgiving Eve, 1972. The film starred my favorite actor, Dick Van Dyke, as Caractacus Potts, father to adorable towheaded twins Jeremy and Jemima. I identified immediately with the children who seemed roughly my age, making it easy to imagine myself alongside them as they dashed across Edwardian England’s green and pleasant land, enjoying their amazing adventures. As for Chitty, what a glorious amalgam of metal and wood and red leather that was. To this day, I’m a sucker for cars with red interiors.


And to this day, I’m still a sucker for Chitty. Which is why, when I learned early this year that one of the two movie cars was in the collection of the Stahls Automotive Foundation in Chesterfield, Michigan, not 30 minutes from my home, I made it my mission to reconnect with my childhood idol.


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


## The Book, the Movie, the Car


*[Chitty Chitty Bang Bang](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/chitty-chitty-bang-bang-turns-50/)* debuted in U.S. theaters on December 18, 1968, and was loosely based on the book written by Ian Fleming, the creator of James Bond. Although it might sound strange that the same person responsible for the world’s best-known spy should also have written a children’s book, compare Bond with Chitty and the similarities are obvious. Like Bond’s gadget-laden Aston Martin DB5, Chitty is full of tricks. Not only was Chitty self-driving, but it was also self-flying and self-motorboating. Even the number plate, GEN11, hints at Chitty’s magical powers (“genie,” get it?). There is travel to exotic locations, nail-biting suspense and harrowing escapes, and merciless villains who are vanquished by a compelling combination of ingenuity and good old British pluck.


LMPC/Getty Images


The book came about after Fleming had suffered a massive heart attack in April 1961. His doctors insisted he convalesce in bed. Even using a typewriter was prohibited. So instead, he took pen and paper and wrote in longhand the bedtime stories he had been telling his young son, Caspar. Fleming took the car’s name from a series of monstrous aero-engined cars that raced in the early 1920s, each named Chitty-Bang-Bang (only one “Chitty” in the name of these original cars).


Count Louis Zborowski driving Chitty Bang Bang 1 to win the Southsea Speed Carnival, 1922.


National Motor Museum/Heritage Images/Getty Images


The cars were built and piloted by the renowned playboy, Count Louis Zborowski. Zborowski’s mother was an Astor and in 1911, when she died and he inherited her fortune, he became one of the richest people in the world under the age of 21. As a boy, Fleming had witnessed Zborowski racing his cars at the storied Brooklands race track in England. He dedicated the book to the count and his car: “To the memory of the original Chitty-Chitty-Bang-Bang, built in 1920 by Count Zborowski on his estate near Canterbury.” The book was illustrated by John Burningham, with Chitty looking vaguely like a Bentley.


Louis Zborowski at the wheel of Chitty Bang Bang I, Brooklands, 1922.


National Motor Museum/Heritage Images/Getty Images


Fleming died on August 12, 1964, at the age of 56, and didn’t live to see the book published. As a tribute to him, his good friend Albert R. “Cubby” Broccoli—producer of the Bond movies—decided to make the book into a movie. Broccoli was a cofounder of EON Productions, which owned the rights to all of Fleming’s works, including Chitty.


Broccoli and his team wanted to make a musical to ride on the tailcoats of the success of Disney movies—specifically, 1964’s *Mary Poppins* —so they signed its male lead, Dick Van Dyke. Broccoli hoped to also enlist Julie Andrews, who had played the title character in Poppins. But she felt the part was too similar to her role as the magical nanny and as the singing nanny in 1965’s *The Sound of Music* . Instead, Sally Ann Howes was cast as Truly Scrumptious, Van Dyke’s love interest in the film. For more of the Poppins magic, Broccoli left nothing to chance and signed the American composing team of Richard and Robert Sherman to write the film’s original songs. The Sherman brothers had won two Oscars in 1965 for *Mary Poppins* (Best Song and Best Score) and would be nominated for another Oscar for Best Song with “Chitty Chitty Bang Bang.”


(L-R) Amanda Slayton, Michaela Pain, art director Peter Lamont, and Broccoli (front), producer of the film.


Central Press/Hulton Archive/Getty Images


Bond veterans Desmond Llewelyn and Gert Frobe joined the cast. Llewelyn, famous for playing Q, Bond’s purveyor of spy gadgets, played Mr. Coggins, the junk man who sells the wrecked Chitty to Caractacus. Frobe, who starred as the villain Auric Goldfinger in 1964’s *Goldfinger* , took the villainous role of Baron Bomburst. Several Bond alumni were behind the camera—which gave some of Chitty’s scenes a distinct Bond vibe—including designer Peter Lamont, special-effects man John Stears, and, most important, production designer Ken Adam.


The word “legend” is often thrown about, but in the case of Sir Ken Adam, it is entirely deserved. Adam was responsible for establishing the epic cinematic style for all the Bond films, beginning in 1962 with *Dr. No* . He created the gold vault and interior layout of Fort Knox in *Goldfinger* and the SPECTRE boardroom from *Thunderball* . Adam was the one who convinced Aston Martin to provide a pre-production DB5 for *Goldfinger* , and, working with special-effects supervisor Stears, he developed the DB5’s myriad gadgets, including the front-mounted machine guns, the revolving license plates, the oil slick, smoke systems, and the ejector passenger seat.


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


When it came to design Chitty, it was only logical that Ken Adam pick up the pen. Much to the chagrin of the book’s illustrator, Adam thought the drawings made Chitty look too normal. He wanted his Chitty to be full of color, a car that looked like it *could* have been built by an eccentric Edwardian inventor, hinting at its magical abilities yet still believable. He based his design on the proportions and character of pre-World War I race cars. Very long hoods for their huge engines; tall, skinny wheels and tires; brass radiators and lamps; and open touring bodies. Adam had his design.


But who would build the actual car? That’s where Alan Mann, one of the most successful team owners in 1960s British motorsports, enters the story.


## Alan Mann Racing: Constructing Chitty


Dean Smith


Founded in 1963 and based in Woking, Surrey, southwest of London,[Alan Mann Racing](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/alan-mann-racing-is-getting-back-to-its-roots-with-the-mk1-escort/) (AMR) became deeply involved in Ford Motor Company’s “Total Performance” campaign of the 1960s and its global assault on motorsports, from rally to touring cars to a lightweight GT40 for endurance racing, and it oversaw the development of the Cobra Daytona coupe.


Alan Mann’s personal ties with Ford’s motorsports maestro Walter Hayes led to some interesting commissions, including involvement with the Fords used in *Goldfinger* . The success of that assignment—and on the Bond films that followed (1965’s *Thunderball* and 1967’s *You Only Live Twice* )—led to Broccoli awarding AMR with the contract to build six different versions of Chitty. He commissioned two road-going models as well as four versions for close-ups, floating sequences, and other special effects. At £80,000 (about $225K, or roughly $2.3M today), it was a big contract for the small but mighty shop.


Dean Smith


Alan Mann Racing is still located in Woking and is today run by Henry, Mann’s youngest son. The focus is still on[Fords of the ’60s](https://www.hagerty.com/media/people/ford-history-repeats-itself-at-alan-mann-racing/) , but the shop also houses the archives that document the construction history of the movie cars. There are boxes upon boxes stuffed with drawings, invoices, and receipts, along with build diaries totaling hundreds of pages. The diary’s first entry is dated Thursday, May 11, 1967: Inquiries were made regarding anodizing aluminum to standard mild steel finish; phone calls were made to Walton Plating in Walton, Derbyshire; and procurement from Ford was organized for rear axle casings, differentials, and axle shafts.


Dean Smith


Dean Smith


Dean Smith


“Ken Adam knew he wanted an Edwardian-looking car with a boat rear end, an appearance that hinted at a boat and a plane, but beyond that, he wasn’t too clear on exactly how the car should look,” recalls Henry today. “Dad went with Ken to visit Stanley Sears, the father of racing driver Jack Sears. Stanley had an enormous collection of fantastic prewar cars, and Dad and Ken went through each of them and chose interesting details off different cars.” Chitty’s dash-mounted oilers and lamps were inspired by a 1904 Mercedes 18/28hp Racing two-seater, for example, while the boa constrictor horn came from a 1903 Clement Talbot Type CT4K 18hp. With its red-painted spoke wheels and red leather interior, the Clement Talbot may have also inspired those features on Chitty, but without documentation, we can only assume.


1903 Clement Talbot Type CT4K 18hp


Chris Stark


1904 Mercedes 18/28hp Racing two-seater


Chris Stark


Once the details were decided, the real work of transforming ideas into reality began. Mann relied heavily upon the various small cottage industries—some literally run from cottages—that still populated Merrie Olde England in those days. The wooden boattail was crafted by Bates Wharf Chertsey, one of the oldest boatyards on the River Thames, with its roots going back to the late 1800s. The car’s aluminum hood and other specialist sheetmetal work were done by Gomm Metalcraft, whose founder, Maurice “Mo” Gomm, had learned his trade during the war years, hand-shaping lightweight alloys to construct Wellington bombers for the Royal Air Force.


After the war, Gomm transitioned to motorsports and later teamed up with Eric Broadley to design and construct the Lola Mk 1 prototype in 1957–58. He built early aluminum monocoque tubs for Tyrrell Racing, the original Williams Formula 1 FX3 chassis, and fabricated oil tanks for the Ford GT40, before he got around to preparing all the AMR Ford Escort body shells and some of Ford’s factory rally cars. Chitty’s distinctive spoked red wheels, meanwhile, were not made of wood but of cast aluminum and were fabricated by Birmingham Aluminium Casting Company, founded in 1903, a firm famous for its pioneering castings of aluminum and magnesium.


Dean Smith


Dean Smith


Dean Smith


Dean Smith


Dean Smith


Lionel Whitehead was one of AMR’s earliest employees, joining in 1964 and working up through 1970, when the original shop closed. Today he’s 95 years old but still has memories of working on the Chitty cars. “I was mainly doing the chassis work for the two roadgoing versions,” he says. “First, we tried using frames from Rolls-Royce hearses. Those weren’t adequate, so we tried using heavy-duty truck frames. Those didn’t work either, so we had to make the entire chassis from scratch.”


Dean Smith


That development included the suspension parts. “I designed the front axle. I had to farm out its construction to a blacksmith,” he explains. “There were 11 parts for that, and then we welded them all up to make a complete axle. The car didn’t have front brakes. The rear brakes were from a Ford Transit Mk 1 van. The rear springs were like truck springs. We ordered them and they made what we wanted.” Whitehead still watches the movie when it’s shown in the U.K., usually every year at Christmas time.


The various frames didn’t go to waste, however. They were used to build some of the race cars seen at the beginning of the film. Another challenge was finding pneumatic tires that could provide some semblance of cushioning for the ride of the 4000-pound behemoth. For the powertrain, AMR used the 3.0-liter V-6 and automatic transmission from a Ford Zephyr.


> Pulling back the magic curtain to reveal the workaday reality does nothing to alter my love for this car.


Dean Smith

## Filming *Chitty* and Its Life After


Principal photography for *Chitty Chitty Bang Bang* began on Monday, July 17, 1967, in England. The start date is significant because it was barely a month after filming had ended for the fifth Bond film, *You Only Live Twice* , and the crew that would shoot Chitty was essentially the same that shot the Bond film: same props crew, same lighting crew, same cameramen, and, of course, Ken Adam.


From the 1968 musical *Chitty Chitty Bang Bang* , cast members (left to right) Dick Van Dyke, Heather Ripley, Adrian Hall, and Sally Ann Howes wave from the flying jalopy.


Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images


The production kicked off its multi-month shoot on the back lots and stages of Pinewood Studios. From this base in Buckinghamshire, the crew went on to film at various nearby locations—such as the famed Cobstone Windmill in Turville that served as the home of the Potts family—before poor weather forced parts of the production to move to the south of France later that summer. AMR delivered the first “standard car” (as the road-going examples were called) on July 26, 1967, just 76 days after work had started on it. Delivery of the second standard came 22 days later, on August 17, 1967.


Victor Crawshaw /Mirrorpix/Getty Images


Victor Crawshaw /Mirrorpix/Getty Images


Henry Mann was a child during AMR’s racing and movie-car heyday, and his father didn’t share much of the business’s day-to-day with him, such that he knew nothing of his dad’s connection to Chitty. “I watched the film as a child, but had no knowledge of Dad’s involvement,” he recalls. “Later on, when my dad’s mom died and we were clearing out her things, there was a little model of Chitty on her dresser. Dad explained everything and I was like, ‘What? And you built a car for the film?!’ That would have been helpful to know when I was a kid on the playground!”


Henry Mann


Dean Smith


To this day, he still marvels at the impact of the movie and its star. “I’m glad it had the power from some small workshop in Surrey to inspire somebody across the pond. I think it was probably a surprise to everybody who worked on Chitty how well-loved the film was and how iconic the car became.”


LMPC/Getty Images


The two road-going versions of Chitty that Alan Mann Racing created still exist. The first standard car (or “Chitty Prime,” as it is sometimes known) was privately owned in England until it was sold in 2011 to Peter Jackson, the director of the *Lord of the Rings* and *The Hobbit* trilogies. It is now part of Jackson’s collection of antique planes and cars in New Zealand. The second standard car (“Chitty Beta”) was used to promote the release of the film in America. This Chitty was displayed in various collections and museums across the country, until it was purchased in May 2021 by the Stahls Automotive Foundation of New Baltimore, Michigan. Once I learned that incredible fact, I reached out to Jeff Stumb, the executive director for the collection, who graciously invited me to a private audience.


## Meeting Your Heroes


Chris Stark


How can I best express how it felt when the garage door rolled open to reveal the car I had dreamed of for more than half a century? I was no longer a 61-year-old geezer—bald, bearded, battered. I had stepped into a time machine where 54 years had evaporated like the bursting of a soap bubble and sent me back to the age of 7.


*Hello, my fine, four-fendered friend…*


Chris Stark


It’s a bit disconcerting with the two dimensions of film now translated into the car’s three-dimensionality. Chitty is much larger in reality, graceful, majestic, and imposing. The proportions are perfect—something not even the best recreated tribute cars can capture—and the details delicious: the beautiful brass, Bugatti-inspired radiator tucked between the swooping curves of the black fenders jauntily pinstriped in red, the mirror-shine polished aluminum of the hood, the soft burnished copper of the exhaust pipe curling through the hood, and the lovely brown strap with the brass buckle to secure it. The interior’s red leather is supple, with the patina of a beloved baseball mitt. Then there is the wooden boattail body, varnished and glowing in rich brown, like the hull of a vintage Chris-Craft motorboat.


> The proportions are perfect and the details delicious.


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


I will be riding shotgun, with Stumb at the wheel, since nobody wants to be known as the guy who crashed Chitty. Like all proper British motorcars, Chitty is right-hand drive. One of the two long brass levers to the right of the driver serves as the selector for the automatic transmission (the other is the handbrake). Since the oversized controls make access to the driver’s seat even more of a challenge, it’s easiest for the driver to enter from the passenger side, so Stumb enters first. There are no front doors, but it’s a bit of a climb up onto the running board and then over the curved cutaway in the wooden body. The car fires up without drama and settles into a soft burble. Sadly, there is none of the chitty-chitty engine clatter or bang-bang backfiring that inspired the name. Stumb slides the lever into drive and we are off.


Our drive takes us on the main road that winds through the collection’s campus. The ride is surprisingly smooth thanks to the car’s long wheelbase. That same wheelbase gives the car, as Dick Van Dyke would later describe, “the turning radius of a battleship.” The steering does not self-center, so after making a turn, Stumb must crank the wheel back to an even keel. The front seat is snug but not uncomfortably so; the rear seat, however, was clearly designed for children. As we motor, I recall Lionel Whitehead saying that Chitty doesn’t have front brakes, so I’m grateful our speeds don’t crest 25 mph. The view down the five-foot hood reflects the blue summer sky. My inner 7-year-old is pinching my 61-year-old self. I’m convinced if Stumb pulled back on the wheel we could take flight.


We remain earthbound.


Chris Stark


> The view down the five-foot hood reflects the blue summer sky. My inner 7-year-old is pinching my 61-year-old self.


When our drive is done, I get the chance to study Chitty in detail. It’s fascinating to see where the movie magic ends and reality begins. Stumb unfastens the leather strap and flips the hood open. Even though I know what to expect, the V-6 looks so laughably small that I actually do laugh. The exhaust pipes that curve so handsomely end at the hood and are not connected to the engine. Looking forward through the engine compartment reveals that the radiator grille is just a grille and not, in fact, a radiator. A tiny electric fan is mounted behind the grille, pointing backwards at the engine’s real radiator for cooling. None of this matters to me; pulling back the magic curtain to reveal the workaday reality does nothing to alter my love for this car.


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


Chris Stark


Why, exactly? Because Chitty is truly a movie car, created through the vision of one man, and the thoughtful expertise of a cottage industry, to translate fantasy to the screen. Other cars in movies are merely that: regular cars that are in movies. Frank Bullitt’s Mustang is just a Mustang. Bandit’s Trans Am is just a Trans Am. Even beneath all the gadgetry, Marty McFly’s DeLorean is at its core a DeLorean. From every angle, though, Chitty is unmistakable and unique. There is only one car that is Chitty, and only one that ever will be.
